newsitem.title: UK: Study find spitting not just rude, but dangerous.
newsitem.headline: Study find spitting not just rude, but dangerous.

text.p: Spitting at someone -- an ancient gesture of contempt -- can be downright dangerous, British doctors reported on Friday.
One man was infected with meningitis after someone spat in his face, Dr Gillian Holdsworth of London's Lewisham Health Authority and colleagues reported in the Lancet Medical Journal.
Saliva and phlegm are known to carry tuberculosis and other germs, but Holdsworth's report shows they can also carry virulent infections.
"One of the reasons they had no-spitting signs in public 40 to 50 years ago was because of the risk of passing on pulmonary tuberculosis," Holdsworth said.
She described the case of a security guard who developed an eye infection after a man spat on him. It turned out to be the bacterium that causes meningitis, a sometimes fatal disease.
"In this instance the manifestation was severe conjunctivitis but could equally well have been systemic meningococcal disease," she wrote in a letter to the Lancet.
The guard and the people he lived with were given antibiotics. The man who spat at him was tracked down and treated, and it turned out he had probably caught the infection from his girlfriend.
"The lesson from this case is that if you are spat on and do not feel well afterwards, remember to tell the doctor what happened," the Lancet said in a statement.
"A lot of people in the community will be carrying meningococci in their throats -- between 20 and 30 percent," Holdsworth said.
